Filing the Form I-765
After receiving the OPT I-20 from OIS, students must file Form I-765 online via their myUSCIS account. If the student does not have an account with USCIS, they must create one.
Important Deadline Considerations
Students must file the Form I-765 within 30 days of the issue date on page 1 of their OPT I-20.
If the student misses this 30-day deadline, they must submit the OPT I-20 Reprint (Missed 30 Days/Date Change) Request in Trojan International before submitting the Form I-765 to USCIS.
Students must file the Form I-765 no more than 60 days after the program end date on page 1 of the OPT I-20.
USCIS will deny the Form I-765 if it is received after either deadline.

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:

USCIS will deny the Form I-765 if it is received after either deadline.
USCIS follows Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) for submission deadlines. Your application must be submitted by 23:59 UTC on the specified deadline, regardless of your local time zone. To avoid denials for missed filing deadlines, we strongly recommend submitting your application at least one day before the due date. Please plan accordingly and confirm UTC conversions for your time zone.
Before You File
Make sure you are physically present in the United States when you file the Form I-765. Filing from outside the United States will result in a denial of your Form I-765.
Ensure your bank account has sufficient funds to cover the non-refundable Form I-765 filing fee to avoid USCIS rejecting your application.
Carefully review our guide to filing Form I-765 for Post-Completion OPT to avoid mistakes that could lead to a rejection, request for evidence or denial of your application. Please note that, in order to access the guide, students must log in using their USC email address when prompted.
Create a myUSCIS account if needed.

How to File the Form I-765
Students will need to upload a copy of the hand-signed OPT I-20 along with other supporting documents and pay the non-refundable Form I-765 filing fee with a credit or debit card.
Students who want a response from USCIS before the estimated processing time can apply for Premium Processing for an additional fee.
To apply for Premium Processing, students can either request it when initially filing the I-765 application or file Form I-907, Request for Premium Processing Service, at a later time. USCIS guarantees a response within 30 business days, not including weekends or holidays, of filing for students who apply for Premium Processing. Attending the required biometrics appointment may reset the processing time. Please refer to the case status section of your myUSCIS portal for additional guidance.

In December 2025, USCIS updated its policy on how photographs are collected and reused for immigration applications.

Photo and Biometric Requirements
In December 2025, USCIS updated its policy on how photographs are collected and reused for immigration applications.
At this time, OPT and STEM OPT applicants must still submit two passport-style photos that meet U.S. Department of State passport photograph requirements, in accordance with current USCIS and OIS instructions.
USCIS may also determine that a new photo is needed and may require a biometrics services appointment at a local Application Support Center. If you receive a biometrics notice or scheduling instructions, you must follow them carefully.
Please regularly check your email, USPS mail and USCIS online account for a biometrics notice and to ensure your mailing address is up to date. If you receive any USCIS notice about photos or biometrics and have questions, submit the Request to Review USCIS Notice and then attend OIS advising for assistance.
If you have been notified that a biometrics appointment will be scheduled but have not received your biometrics appointment notice within two weeks, you should submit a USCIS Case Inquiry for Non-Delivery of Notice.

USCIS has expanded the use of social media review in certain immigration applications. As a result, officers will conduct a closer review of a student’s immigration history and compliance with U.S. laws and students’ online activity may be considered as part of USCIS’s vetting process.
Promoting or supporting anti-American or antisemitic views will be considered serious negative factors and may lead to a denial of the application. The new policy is effective Aug. 19, 2025, and applies to both pending requests and those filed on or after that date.

If you receive one of these notices, you must submit the Request to Review USCIS Notice to receive further guidance. After submitting the form, an advisor will review your case and follow up with the next steps.
Rejection
If an application is rejected, the student will receive an I-797C Notice of Action: Rejection. USCIS will indicate the reason for rejection on the I-797C. A student who receives a rejection notice should:
Submit the Request to Review USCIS Notice.
Meet with an advisor during OIS drop-in advising to determine eligibility to resubmit Form I-765.
If eligible, request an updated OPT I-20 using the OPT I-20 Reprint Request in Trojan International.

A student may receive a Request for Evidence (RFE) if USCIS needs more information before processing their application, such as if the payment method was not accepted. The RFE will specify which additional documents are required and the specific deadline for responding. The student will need to submit the Request to Review USCIS Notice before responding to the RFE.
Notice of Intent to Deny
Upon review of the supporting evidence, USCIS may identify concerns and issue a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID). This warning letter allows students to provide any new evidence addressing the concerns noted. The NOID includes a response deadline and failure to respond by that date can result in a denial of their application. The student will need to submit the Request to Review USCIS Notice before responding to the NOID.

Maintaining F-1 Status While on OPT
General OPT Requirements
In addition to complying with U.S. laws and immigration requirements, failure to meet the following requirements for OPT employment may result in the automatic termination of the student’s SEVIS record by SEVP and/or USCIS.
Direct Relation to Major
Any employment on OPT must be directly related to the student’s major. USCIS determines whether a job is related. Therefore, the student should be able to:
Provide an explanation to USCIS if asked how their job is related to their major at USC.
On a day-to-day basis, they apply the knowledge they gained from their academic program to their job.
Students will use the following template as a guide if needed in the future: “I work [insert full-time or part-time] as a [insert job title] for [insert employer name]. My duties include [insert list of job duties]. At this job, I use [insert list of relevant skills/knowledge from your coursework], which directly relates to my USC [insert degree level] in [insert field of study].”
Hours of Employment

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:
levant skills/knowledge from your coursework], which directly relates to my USC [insert degree level] in [insert field of study].”
Hours of Employment
The student must work at least 20 hours per week. If the student has more than one employer, the total number of hours among all employers must be at least 20.
Types of Employment Permitted While on OPT
The following types of employment are permitted while a student is on OPT:
Standard, full-time employer: Student works for one employer for at least 20 hours per week.
Multiple employers: Student works for more than one employer, with a combined total of at least 20 hours per week.
Multiple short-term employers: Musicians or other performing artists may work for multiple short-term employers (i.e., gigs). Students should maintain a list of all gigs, including the dates and durations.
Work for hire/contract: Also commonly referred to as “1099 employment,” the term “work for hire” describes a service based on a contractual agreement rather than an employment relationship. This means that the individual is performing a service.

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:
” describes a service based on a contractual agreement rather than an employment relationship. This means that the individual is performing a service.
Self-employment: A student may start a business and be self-employed. The student must be able to prove to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security that they have the proper business licenses and are actively engaged in a business related to their degree program. OIS recommends that a self-employed student consult a lawyer.
Employment through an employment/staffing agency or consulting firm: A student may gain employment through a third-party agency.
Unpaid/volunteer jobs: A student may work on a volunteer basis or as an unpaid intern, where this does not violate any U.S. labor laws. Labor laws vary by state. Check with the company’s human resources department for restrictions.
Unemployment
Unemployment days will start to accrue on the approved EAD start date. If the requested start date has passed without approval, unemployment days will not start with the originally requested date.

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:
approved EAD start date. If the requested start date has passed without approval, unemployment days will not start with the originally requested date.
A student cannot exceed 90 days of unemployment during their authorized Post-Completion OPT period. A student who accrues more than 90 days of unemployment is in violation of their F-1 status and should join OIS drop-in advising to discuss their options with an advisor.
OPT Reporting Requirements
U.S. Address Update
While on OPT, students must submit the SEVIS U.S. Address and Contact Update via Trojan International within 10 days of any change in their U.S. address. Please note that updating your home address does not automatically update your OPT employment if you are working remotely from home.
Reporting Employment Update to OIS
To maintain F-1 status while on approved OPT, students are required to report any change in employment within 10 days. All updates must be submitted to OIS through the OPT Employment Update Form in Trojan International.
The student must report the following changes:
Adding new employer(s).
Changes to current employment, such as:
Job title
Employer name

Options for F-1 Students After OPT Ends
Once a student reaches the end of their Post-Completion OPT authorization period, they will have a 60-day grace period to remain in the United States and prepare for their next steps.
STEM OPT Extension
A graduate currently on Post-Completion OPT may be eligible for a 24-month extension of their work authorization if they have earned a bachelor’s, master’s or doctoral degree in an eligible STEM field, as designated by USCIS. A student is eligible to apply up to 90 days before the end date listed on their EAD, and must apply before that end date. For more information, visit our STEM OPT Extension page.
New Program of Study at USC
Students must apply to their new program, be admitted and be issued a new I-20 from the USC Graduate Admission office before the end of the grace period. Proof of funding is required to issue the new I-20. Please contact the USC Graduate Admission office with questions regarding I-20 issuance, as OIS does not oversee the issuance of these I-20s.
Transfer to Another Institution

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:
Graduate Admission office with questions regarding I-20 issuance, as OIS does not oversee the issuance of these I-20s.
Transfer to Another Institution
Students must apply to another institution, be admitted and have their USC SEVIS record transferred out to the new institution before the end of the 60-day grace period. In addition, the start date at the transfer-in school must be within five months of the last date the student is on OPT. Students also must report their employment end date for the current employer(s) through the OPT employment update before requesting a transfer. For instructions on requesting a SEVIS transfer, refer to our page on attending another institution.
Depart the United States
Students may choose to depart the United States upon completion of their STEM OPT. They must depart by the end of their 60-day grace period.
Change of Status
If eligible for another nonimmigrant or immigrant status, students may apply for a change of status with USCIS. USCIS must receive the application to change the immigration status before the end of the grace period.

Optional Practical Training FAQ
My city of birth is incorrect on my OPT I-20 and/or past I-20s. What should I do?
The city of birth information was added to your initial USC I-20 based on the information you entered and verified in your USC Admissions record. To update or correct the city of birth in your SEVIS record, please submit the City of Birth Correction Request.
Your OPT I-20 with the current/incorrect city of birth information can be submitted to USCIS along with the other OPT application materials, as it will not negatively affect your OPT application. A reprint of your OPT I-20 is not necessary, as your SEVIS record will contain the correct information.
I applied for a Reduced Course Load (RCL) this semester, but the “Authorized Reduced Course Load” section on my I-20 is blank. Should I be concerned?
No, it is fine if your RCL was approved but the “Authorized Reduced Course Load” is blank. Please disregard this section as it is not needed for OPT application purposes.

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:
ur RCL was approved but the “Authorized Reduced Course Load” is blank. Please disregard this section as it is not needed for OPT application purposes.
The current session start and end dates on my I-20 are incorrect. Does this need to be corrected?
No, it is fine if your current session start and end dates are for a previous semester. Please disregard these dates as it will not impact your OPT application.
Do I need to include copies of my initial I-20 from USC, or of any other I-20s that do not show CPT or OPT work authorization, in my USCIS application?
No, only include copies of I-20s with work authorization.
How do I submit the Form I-765 and supporting OPT documents to USCIS?
Students must submit their OPT application, including Form I-765 and supporting documents, to USCIS online via their myUSCIS account. Refer to our Post-Completion OPT page for required documents and submission instructions.
How do I write my CPT and/or past OPT employment information in the “Additional Information” sections of the online Form I-765?

How do I write my CPT and/or past OPT employment information in the “Additional Information” sections of the online Form I-765?
Students who have previously received work authorization (including CPT, OPT, STEM OPT, or economic hardship employment authorization) must use the “Additional Information” section of the online Form I-765 to provide details of any prior employment authorization.
This is located under:

Students should list:

Do I need to use my USC email address for myUSCIS account? What happens to my USC email address when I graduate?
No, you may use any personal email address of your choosing. This could be your USC email or a non-USC email. However, USC IT will keep the USC emails of students on or pending approval for OPT/STEP OPT active.
For questions related to accessing your @usc.edu email address after graduation, refer to the USC Alumni Association’s FAQ (select “Alumni Email” tab).
Note that your SEVP Portal account creation link will be sent to your USC email address on or after your OPT EAD start date. Please monitor your USC email for this link around your EAD start date. As a reminder, the SEVP Portal is for view access only and all updates should be made via Trojan International.

Please attend drop-in advising to speak with an OIS advisor.
What is the USCIS processing time for OPT applications?
Please refer to our Post-Completion OPT page.
My OPT I-20 does not have a travel endorsement on pages 2 or 3. Is this a problem?
No, a travel signature is not required to apply for OPT.
My prior CPT information is not printed on my OPT I-20. Is this an error?
No, your OPT I-20 will only show CPT, which is for the current semester. It will not be printed on the I-20 if it was completed in a prior semester.
Can I travel while my OPT application is pending?
Filing for Post-Completion OPT has no effect on students’ ability to travel internationally and return to the United States before their I-20 program end date (i.e., graduation date). Prior to the graduation date, the student is a current student for travel purposes. Students are strongly advised against traveling internationally after their I-20 program end date until they have received their EAD. Please refer to the travel section of the OIS website for guidance.

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:
ernationally after their I-20 program end date until they have received their EAD. Please refer to the travel section of the OIS website for guidance.
Can I enroll in classes while on OPT?
Per immigration regulations, students cannot be enrolled in certificate or degree-seeking programs (in-person or online) while on OPT. Students may take classes that are avocational or recreational and incidental to their employment. For example, a student with a computer science major could take a class in a foreign language for personal development.
There’s a mistake on my OPT EAD due to a USCIS error. What should I do?
If your OPT EAD contains an error due to a mistake made by USCIS, you will not be required to file a new Form I-765 or pay the application filing fee. To request a replacement EAD due to a USCIS error, follow these steps:
Request a reprint of your I-20 showing your OPT is approved by submitting an I-20 Reprint Request.
Make a photocopy of the incorrect EAD — you must keep a copy on file for your personal records.
Assemble the following documents:
The original card containing the error.
A detailed letter of explanation of the card error.

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS

r your personal records.
Assemble the following documents:
The original card containing the error.
A detailed letter of explanation of the card error.
Copy of the most recently issued OPT I-20.
Supporting documentation on the correct information (e.g., a copy of the passport bio page).
Mail your request to the center that processed your OPT application and make sure you get a tracking number. Check the USCIS website for the most up to date addresses.
Students who applied for OPT via Premium Processing and received an incorrect EAD due to a USCIS error should email psc-premium.processing@uscis.dhs.gov, explain the situation and attach a scanned copy of your EAD with the error for further guidance from USCIS.
My OPT EAD got lost or stolen. What should I do?
If your OPT EAD has been lost, stolen, or damaged, you will need to pay the application filing fee again and submit a replacement EAD application to USCIS. To file for a replacement EAD, follow these steps:
Request a reprint of your I-20 showing your OPT is approved by submitting an I-20 Reprint Request.
Submit a new Form I-765 online to USCIS, following the Guide to Filing Form I-765 with USCIS, noting the following changes:

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:
g an I-20 Reprint Request.
Submit a new Form I-765 online to USCIS, following the Guide to Filing Form I-765 with USCIS, noting the following changes:
What is your reason for applying? Select “Replacement of lost, stolen, or damaged employment authorization document.”
Have you previously filed Form I-765? Select “Yes.”
Include a copy of the most recently issued OPT I-20, a copy of the I-797 OPT Approval Notice and (if you have it) a copy of your OPT EAD.
You will be required to pay the Form I-765 filing fee again.
USCIS will process your EAD replacement request within about three months.
Can students file an OPT application with USCIS while abroad?
No, students must be present in the United States at the time of the OPT application submission. Otherwise, the OPT will be denied.
Can students work remotely on OPT?
Yes, students may work remotely in another state within the United States. Remote work outside of the United States is not permitted, as OPT is a work authorization for work in the United States. Students must report their remote address as their employer’s onsite address and continue to comply with all OPT reporting requirements.

chunks.title: Post-Completion OPT - USC OIS
chunks.text:
nited States. Students must report their remote address as their employer’s onsite address and continue to comply with all OPT reporting requirements.
I failed to graduate but my Post-Completion OPT application was approved by USCIS. What should I do?
You must complete your degree requirements in the upcoming semester. You must work part-time (20 or fewer hours per week) while you retake your class. Please join a drop-in advising session to speak with an OIS advisor if this has occurred.
What time zone does USCIS use for the I-765 filing deadline?
USCIS follows Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) for submission deadlines. UTC is typically seven to eight hours ahead of Pacific Time, depending on whether Daylight Saving Time or Standard Time is in effect. To avoid missing your filing deadline, we strongly recommend submitting your Form I-765 at least one day in advance of the due date.
I logged in to my USCIS account to check the status of my pending OPT application, and under the “myProgress” tab, it says the estimated decision time is nine months. Is this accurate?

While your USCIS account may show an estimated decision time of nine months under the “myProgress” tab, the typical processing time for OPT applications is still approximately three to four months, provided there are no errors or issues with your application.
I received a biometrics notice from USCIS. What should I do?
If USCIS does not have a recent, acceptable photo on file, they will require a Biometrics Services Appointment (BSA) at a local Application Support Center (ASC). Check your email, USPS mail and USCIS online account regularly after you file your Form I-765 for a biometrics notice and ensure your U.S. mailing address is up to date. If you receive any USCIS notice about photos or biometrics, follow the instructions provided on that notice. If you have any questions regarding the notice, submit the Request to Review USCIS Notice in Trojan International.

University Compliance Requirements
USC must comply with federal laws, U.S. Department of State regulations and U.S. Department of Homeland Security regulations related to nonimmigrant visa holders engaged in academic activities — most often F-1 and J-1 visa holders. USC values international students’ and scholars’ contributions to the furtherance of the university’s mission. The Form I-17 and What It Means For Departments
What Is the Form I-17?
The Form I-17 is the official SEVP certification record and petition maintained with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that authorizes USC to issue the Form I-20 and enroll F-1 nonimmigrant students. This petition also identifies the institution’s approved locations, programs and Designated School Officials (DSOs).

What It Means For Departments
USC may issue Form I-20s only for academic programs that are approved and listed on its Form I-17. Any changes to an existing program — such as program length, required units for degree completion or other material modifications — or the addition of a new academic program must be reviewed and approved through an update to the Form I-17 before Form I-20s can be issued for that program. Failure to comply with SEVP regulations may jeopardize the university’s SEVP certification.

chunks.title: Student Visa Types - USC OIS
chunks.text:
Student Visa Types — USC OIS
Student Visa Types
What Is a Visa?
A citizen of a foreign country who seeks to enter the United States generally must first obtain a U.S. visa, which is placed in the traveler’s passport. For international students, the F-1 and J-1 visas are the primary categories. Usually, the F-1 visa is issued to students enrolled in full-time academic programs at accredited U.S. institutions, while the J-1 visa is for students participating in approved exchange programs. Both visas allow students to seek entry in order to study legally in the United States.
How to Read and Understand Your Visa
Please use the illustrated guide below to learn how to read your visa and ensure that all information is correct.
Additional Visa Information
1. Surname and Given Name
Check that your name is spelled correctly. Both your given name and surname (family name) should match the names on the biometric page of your passport.
2. Issuing Post Name
The U.S. embassy or consulate where your visa was issued.
3. Sex
This should match the sex on your passport.
4. Birth Date
Check that your date of birth is correct and matches the one on your passport.
5. Control Number

chunks.title: Student Visa Types - USC OIS
chunks.text:
should match the sex on your passport.
4. Birth Date
Check that your date of birth is correct and matches the one on your passport.
5. Control Number
The visa control number is generally not important for the average visa holder; it’s an internal tracking number used by the U.S. Department of State.
6. Visa
“R” indicates a regular passport, while “D” or “O” would be used for diplomatic or official passports, respectively.
7. Type/Class
This indicates the visa category and the purpose of your travel.
8. Visa Number
This red number is generally printed at the bottom right of newer visa documents and usually contains eight digits.
9. Expiration Date
The last day you may use your visa to seek entry into the United States. It has nothing to do with how long you may stay in the United States.
10. Issue Date
The date the U.S. embassy or consulate issued your visa stamp.
11. Annotation
This section may include additional information about your visa. For example, on a student visa, it will show your SEVIS number and your school’s name.
12. Entries

chunks.title: Student Visa Types - USC OIS
chunks.text:
may include additional information about your visa. For example, on a student visa, it will show your SEVIS number and your school’s name.
12. Entries
“M” means that you can seek entry into the United States multiple times. If there is a number here, you may apply for entry that many times. “S” stands for single entry.
13. Passport Number
Check that this number matches the number in your passport.
Common Student Visa Types
F-1 Student Visa
J-1 Student Visa
Eligibility
The F-1 visa is the most common student visa type. It is issued to students who are admitted to a full-time academic or language program at a U.S. institution.
The J-1 visa is an exchange visitor visa type. It is issued to students who are admitted to a full-time academic or language program at a U.S. institution.
Document Provided by USC for Visa Application
The Graduate Admission office issues Form I-20s, the official three-page document that is endorsed by a Designated School Official, to admitted students.
Once students receive their Form I-20, they can apply for the F-1 visa at a U.S. embassy or consulate in their home country.

Renewing Your Passport or F/J Visa
On This Page
Jump to a Section
Renewing Your Passport
All nonimmigrants in the United States are required to maintain a valid passport at all times. Passports should be valid for at least six months into the future when entering and reentering the United States and also when applying for a visa.
Students and scholars should contact their local embassy or consulate for instructions on renewing their passports.
Students and scholars whose passports have expired but whose visas remain valid may still use that visa if they still have the old passports. Remember to carry and present both the old and new passports when traveling.
Back to Top
Renewing Your F/J Visa
Students and scholars may stay in the United States on an expired F-1 or J-1 visa as long as they maintain their immigration status by having a valid Form I-20 or DS-2019 and an I-94 Arrival/Departure Record.

chunks.title: Renewing Your Passport or F/J Visa - USC OIS
chunks.text:
expired F-1 or J-1 visa as long as they maintain their immigration status by having a valid Form I-20 or DS-2019 and an I-94 Arrival/Departure Record.
If students and scholars are traveling and will not use automatic revalidation to reenter the United States, they must have a valid visa. Students and scholars who need to renew their F-1 or J-1 visa abroad must schedule an appointment with a U.S. embassy or consulate as soon as possible due to increased security clearance and visa processing times.
Due to a presidential proclamation issued in June 2025, students holding passports from certain countries are currently not eligible to apply for an F-1 or J-1 visa.
Canadian and Bermudian citizens do not need to obtain an F-1 or J-1 visa to study in the United States. However, they must present a valid passport, a USC-issued Form I-20 or DS-2019, proof of SEVIS fee payment and evidence of financial support at the U.S. Port of Entry where they are admitted in F-1 or J-1 status. They must satisfy all standard admission requirements at the U.S. Port of Entry to be admitted in F-1 or J-1 status.

chunks.text:

We recommend setting your social media accounts to “public,” as the U.S. Department of State now reviews publicly available social media content as part of its visa screening and vetting process. Keeping your profiles public can help avoid delays or additional scrutiny during processing.
Interview Locations
The U.S. Department of State requires nonimmigrant visa applicants to schedule and attend their U.S. visa interviews at a U.S. embassy or consulate located in either their country of citizenship or residence. Visas cannot be renewed inside the United States.
Additionally, consider the following when choosing your visa interview location:
If applying in a country based on residency (rather than citizenship), applicants must provide evidence of legal residence in that country.
Applicants are strongly encouraged to email the U.S. embassy or consulate with any questions about residency-based eligibility before the appointment.

chunks.title: Renewing Your Passport or F/J Visa - USC OIS
chunks.text:
Applicants are strongly encouraged to email the U.S. embassy or consulate with any questions about residency-based eligibility before the appointment.
For nationals of countries where the United States does not maintain routine immigrant or nonimmigrant visa operations, applicants must apply at designated U.S. embassies or consulates. If this applies to you, verify whether you need a visa to enter that country before making plans.
If you are a Mexican or Canadian citizen or resident and your visa application is denied, automatic revalidation does not apply.
Once students and scholars have made a visa interview appointment at a U.S. embassy or consulate abroad, they should review the embassy or consulate’s website for details on the visa renewal process, including required documents.
Wait Times
Students and scholars can check visa wait times at U.S. embassies and consulates through the U.S. Department of State website. Given the high demand for appointments at most U.S. embassies and consulates, schedule your appointment as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Renewing Your Passport or F/J Visa - USC OIS
chunks.text:
artment of State website. Given the high demand for appointments at most U.S. embassies and consulates, schedule your appointment as soon as possible.
Due to security checks, administrative processing and significant visa processing backlogs at many U.S. embassies and consulates, the short winter or spring recess may not allow enough time to receive clearance and a renewed visa and to return before classes resume. OIS strongly advises against traveling during these breaks if your visa has expired; instead, contact OIS with any questions or issues.
Fees
The visa issuance fee, also known as the reciprocity fee, depends on the applicant’s country of citizenship and is based on reciprocal agreements between the United States and that country. Students from certain countries must pay this fee for all initial F and J visa applications and renewals. Not all countries have a reciprocity fee.
This fee is separate from the nonimmigrant visa application fee (MRV). Fees and policies can change, so always check the most current information on the U.S. Department of State website.
Visa Reciprocity

chunks.title: Renewing Your Passport or F/J Visa - USC OIS
chunks.text:
cation fee (MRV). Fees and policies can change, so always check the most current information on the U.S. Department of State website.
Visa Reciprocity
According to the U.S. Department of State Foreign Affairs Manual: “INA 221(c) and INA 281 require the Department to set visa validity, number of entries, and fees for nationals of a country based on what that country provides to U.S. citizens for the same purpose of travel. The goal of visa reciprocity is to obtain visa regimes consistent with U.S. laws, regulations, and national interests and to encourage international travel that benefits U.S. travelers and business.”
The U.S. Department of State maintains online visa reciprocity schedules for each country for which it issues visas.
Visa Interview Waiver Policy
F-1 students should expect to attend an in-person visa interview when applying for an F-1 visa, including most renewals.
Under the current U.S. Department of State policy, F-1 applicants are no longer among the categories that are generally eligible for an interview waiver, although consular officers retain discretion in individual cases.

Applying for Your Visa (Students) — USC OIS
Applying for Your Visa (Students)
How to Apply for a Visa
Step 1: Receive Documents From the USC Graduate Admission Office
If you’re applying for an F-1 visa, you’ll receive a Form I-20. If you’re applying for a J-1 visa, you’ll receive a Form DS-2019.
Step 2: Pay the Mandatory SEVIS I-901 Fee
Every international student or exchange visitor who wishes to begin an “initial” program of study or research must pay the SEVIS I-901 fee to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. You will need information from your USC Form I-20 or DS-2019 when paying the fee. Print the fee payment receipt to present at the visa interview and at the U.S. Port of Entry.
Step 3: Complete the DS-160 Visa Application*
Visit the U.S. Department of State’s website to complete the application. Find out more about the required documents below. Here are some tips for completing the application:
Use only the “back” and “next” buttons that are part of the application — not your web browser’s arrows.
Be as accurate as possible with any questions asked.
Do not submit the application until it is complete.

chunks.title: Applying for Your Visa (Students) - USC OIS
chunks.text:
application — not your web browser’s arrows.
Be as accurate as possible with any questions asked.
Do not submit the application until it is complete.
At the end of the online application, print the confirmation page with the barcode, as it is required for all phases of the interview.
Step 4: Schedule and Complete a Visa Interview at a U.S. Embassy or Consulate
To obtain the most current and accurate information on the visa application and interview process, international students should review the website of the U.S. consulate or embassy where they will schedule their visa interview.
Check out the interview tips below to prepare.
Step 5: Arrive at a U.S. Airport and Clear Customs at a U.S. Port of Entry
You will need these documents:
Original I-20 or DS-2019
Valid passport
F-1 or J-1 student visa stamp in passport*
SEVIS fee payment receipt
Financial documents consistent with Form I-20 or DS-2019

chunks.title: Applying for Your Visa (Students) - USC OIS
chunks.text:

Valid passport
F-1 or J-1 student visa stamp in passport*
SEVIS fee payment receipt
Financial documents consistent with Form I-20 or DS-2019
*Canadian and Bermudian citizens do not need to obtain an F-1 or J-1 visa to study in the United States. However, they must present a valid passport, a USC-issued Form I-20 or DS-2019, proof of SEVIS fee payment and evidence of financial support at the U.S. Port of Entry where they are admitted in F-1 or J-1 status. They must satisfy all standard admission requirements at the U.S. Port of Entry to be admitted in F-1 or J-1 status.
Required Documents for a Visa Application
In general, all applicants for a student visa must provide the following documents.
F-1 Students
J-1 Students
All four pages of USC Form I-20
Both pages of USC Form DS-2019
Confirmation receipt showing completed nonimmigrant visa application Form DS-160 with the assigned ID number
Passport valid for at least six months after the proposed date of entry into the United States
Visa processing fee payment receipt
SEVIS I-901 fee payment receipt
Proof of funding for amounts listed on the I-20 or DS-2019
⚠ Don’t Forget: Double-Check the Name on Your Passport

chunks.title: Applying for Your Visa (Students) - USC OIS
chunks.text:
eipt

⚠ Don’t Forget: Double-Check the Name on Your Passport
In addition to being valid for at least six months after the student’s proposed date of entry into the United States, the student’s passport should:
Have a name that accurately reflects the student’s formal name.
Have a name that is broken out into separate lines for the given (first) name and the family (last) name, unless there is only one name and no family name.
How to Prepare for a Visa Interview
To obtain a student visa, you will need to attend an interview at a U.S. embassy or consulate. Here are some tips to keep in mind:
Be brief. Interviews are typically around five minutes long. Because of this, it’s best to keep answers and explanations short and to the point.
Speak in English. Practice interviewing in English with a native English speaker. Being fluent and confident will help you during the interview. However, avoid preparing a speech.
Speak for yourself. Having parents or others speak on a student’s behalf does not make a good impression on the consular officer, so make sure to make your case independently.

chunks.title: Applying for Your Visa (Students) - USC OIS
chunks.text:
g parents or others speak on a student’s behalf does not make a good impression on the consular officer, so make sure to make your case independently.
Keep documents organized. It should be immediately clear to the consular officer what written documents you are presenting and what they signify. Lengthy written explanations cannot be read or evaluated quickly.
Stay positive. Do not argue with the consular officer and avoid coming across as rude or sarcastic, even if the visa application is denied.
How to Show Ties to Your Home Country
Occasionally, students are denied visas if the consular officer is not sufficiently convinced of their intention to return to their home country after completing their studies. This is based on Section 214(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act that states: “Every alien shall be presumed to be an immigrant until he establishes to the satisfaction of the consular officer, at the time of application for admission, that he is entitled to a nonimmigrant status…”

chunks.title: Applying for Your Visa (Students) - USC OIS
chunks.text:
l he establishes to the satisfaction of the consular officer, at the time of application for admission, that he is entitled to a nonimmigrant status…”
Applicants from countries facing economic problems, or from countries where many nationals have remained in the United States as immigrants, will have more difficulty obtaining visas. They are also more likely to be asked about job opportunities at home after their stay in the United States.
This means that international students must prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that they have a “permanent residence” or “strong ties” to their home country, thereby demonstrating that they do not intend to immigrate to, or obtain residency or citizenship in, the United States. Fortunately, a visa denial is not permanent and can be reversed if the student can show new, irrefutable evidence.
Here are some ways to demonstrate strong ties to your home country:
Convince the consular officer that the sole (not just primary) purpose of the visit to the United States is to pursue a program of study.
Outline post-graduation plans upon returning to your home country.
Document family ties, business interests and assets in your home country.

chunks.title: Applying for Your Visa (Students) - USC OIS
chunks.text:
of study.
Outline post-graduation plans upon returning to your home country.
Document family ties, business interests and assets in your home country.
Discuss job prospects in your home country upon completion of a U.S. education.
Social Media
Once you submit your visa application, we recommend making your social media accounts public, as the U.S. Department of State now reviews publicly available social media content as part of the visa screening and vetting process. Keeping your profiles public can help avoid delays or additional scrutiny during processing.
What to Do if Your Visa Application Is Pending or Denied
Students who are not able to enter the United States in time for USC’s Welcome Trojans Orientation due to visa delays or denials should contact the Office of Orientation Programs and their academic department to alert them of the delay.

chunks.title: Applying for Your Visa (Students) - USC OIS
chunks.text:
Orientation due to visa delays or denials should contact the Office of Orientation Programs and their academic department to alert them of the delay.
In general, a student cannot arrive more than one week after classes start and still be enrolled for that semester. Students who may be more than one week late will need to work with their academic department and the admissions office to defer their attendance to the next semester. The Graduate Admissions office will then assist students with getting an updated Form I-20 or DS-2019.
Pending Application
Visa applications may be in pending status due to security clearances being performed by the U.S. Department of State. There are often longer delays for security checks in China and Iran. It is not possible to expedite the security clearance process, and USC is unable to intervene on the student’s behalf.
Denied Application
Common reasons for a visa application denial are:
Section 221(g): Lack of required documentation.
INA 214(b): Failure to demonstrate eligibility for the visa category being applied for (insufficient “ties to home country” is a possible reason).
If you receive a denial:

chunks.title: Applying for Your Visa (Students) - USC OIS
chunks.text:
o demonstrate eligibility for the visa category being applied for (insufficient “ties to home country” is a possible reason).
If you receive a denial:
Request written documentation for the reason of denial if you don’t get a letter explaining why the application has been denied.
Politely ask the officer how to improve your chances for next time and what additional documentation should be provided to reverse the denial.
Thank the consular officer and take down their name for future reference.
Do not get upset or argue with the consular officer.

Applying for Your Visa (Scholars)
The U.S. J-1 Exchange Visitor Program promotes educational and cultural exchange between international scholars and the U.S. academic community. If you are an exchange visitor who is already in the United States and would like to transfer to USC, please refer to our instructions for transferring to USC.

chunks.text:
ResNet is USC Housing’s residential network for all residents of university housing buildings. Both high speed wireless and Ethernet connections are available.
Getting Connected
USC Secured Wireless
It is usually simple to connect your computer to the university wireless network. Visit the Information Technology Services Wireless page to get instructions based on your computer’s operating system.
Wired Ethernet Connection
Make sure your USC e-mail is activated:
You probably activated your e-mail account during orientation at the first login website. If you have not already done so, then please visit www.usc.edu/firstlogin. Activation of your account may take from one to two hours. You will use the username and password that was created with your first login to connect to ResNet. (Note: your username is usually your email address without the “@usc.edu” at the end).
Register your Ethernet card:

chunks.title: ResNet | USC Housing
chunks.text:
first login to connect to ResNet. (Note: your username is usually your email address without the “@usc.edu” at the end).
Register your Ethernet card:
If your computer has not connected to the network before, it will need to be registered. To do so, simply plug it into the Ethernet jack provided for you in your room and open your Internet browser. You should be automatically taken to the Network Registration Page. Then enter your USC username and password to register your computer. After registration, your connection should immediately become available.
If you cannot connect:
Make sure you have an Ethernet port. If it is not built in, make sure that your card is properly installed.
Check your cord for any damage and make sure that it is plugged into the correct port on your computer. Also, check to see that it is plugged into the wall correctly. Verify that you did not accidentally plug it into the phone jack. The Ethernet jack will be colored, the phone jack will be white. Try disabling any wireless connections, as these may interfere with you connecting to ResNet.
Additional ResNet information can be found at the Information Technology Services Wired Connection page.

chunks.title: Furnishings | USC Housing
chunks.text:
With the variety of buildings and room types offered by USC Housing, furniture varies, but all facilities are fully furnished.
Furniture
All university housing facilities come with basic furniture (beds, chairs, tables, etc.) appropriate to the room type. Residents will need to bring basic household items with them. Please review our “What to Bring with You” page for more information
Apartments with living rooms are furnished with a couch, armchair, coffee table and in some cases, end tables.
Every resident is provided with a bed, desk, desk chair, three-drawer dresser and closet space.
In all undergraduate and graduate buildings with shared bedrooms, beds are extra-long twin size (measuring 36” x 80”). Single occupancy bedrooms in graduate housing have a full-sized, extra-long bed (measuring 54″ x 80″).
Kitchens
Apartments with full kitchens are equipped with a sink, stove and full-sized refrigerator (no microwave or other appliances) and include a dining table and chairs.
Smaller format apartments, such as the two-bedroom loft units in University Village or bachelor units have a smaller kitchenette.

chunks.title: Assignments and Contracts | USC Housing
chunks.text:
Please note: the information below is for new students only.
Assignments
We can offer housing assignments only to certified students. To be certified, you must have submitted your USC Enrollment Commitment Deposit form and the $300 enrollment deposit, or approved waiver, to the Office of Admission.
First-year freshmen (defined by USC Housing as recent high school graduates with no college credits), whose housing applications are received by USC Housing on or before May 1, are guaranteed housing. However, this is not a guarantee of a particular type of assignment or a specific building. Early receipt of your housing application increases your chances of being assigned to one of your building or program preferences; it does not guarantee it.
We are unable to guarantee housing to transferring undergraduate, new graduate students or continuing non-resident students. Assignments for those applicants are made based on application date and availability.
Space Assignment
The USC Housing Services Office makes assignments based on the following criteria:
The date your application is received by USC Housing Services

chunks.title: Assignments and Contracts | USC Housing
chunks.text:
nment
The USC Housing Services Office makes assignments based on the following criteria:
The date your application is received by USC Housing Services
Available spaces in the buildings or programs you have requested and for which you are eligible
Your assignment will be as close to your requests as possible, based on availability and eligibility; however, there is a possibility that this contract may not match any of your building preferences. (Please note that your room or apartment number is not part of your contract and subject to change without notice.)
Roommate Assignments
If you requested specific roommates and USC Housing was able to assign you together, that roommate(s) will display on the online portal.
If you did not request a specific roommate, and you are a new freshman who applied by the early May application deadline, your roommate(s) will be assigned based on gender, building assignment and the information in the “Your Profile” section of your housing application.

chunks.title: Sample Costs | USC Housing
chunks.text:
How much will living in university housing cost you? Here are estimated university-billed living yearly expenses for undergraduates:
Freshmen
Estimated yearly living expenses for 2026-2027, (two semesters of rent, default required full meal plans and optional parking) range from $22,608 to $23,608 for the more common suite and residence hall double room types and $23,408 to $24,808. Rents for some assignments, especially single-occupancy room types, are higher and will affect the yearly cost. Cable and Internet connections, and all utilities, are included in all buildings.
Upperclassmen
For upperclassmen, the estimated per-year living expenses for 2026-2027 (two semesters of rent, default partial required meal plans and optional parking) range from $16,538 to $19,218 for the more common apartment types in a double-occupancy room. Rents for some assignments, especially single-occupancy room types, are higher and will affect the yearly cost. Cable and Internet connections, and all utilities, are included in all undergraduate buildings.

chunks.title: Sample Costs | USC Housing
chunks.text:
oom types, are higher and will affect the yearly cost. Cable and Internet connections, and all utilities, are included in all undergraduate buildings.
Estimates do not include items such as groceries for those living in assignments without full meal plans or personal incidentals. Actual costs will vary.
USC Hospitality’s website offers most information about the meal plans available to USC students.
Additional information about the cost of attending USC can be found on the university’s financial aid page.

As an added service, USC Housing provides printers in every CSC’s lobby for residents’ use. Your USCard ID will be used to activate your print jobs and track your Housing Print Balance.
At the beginning of each semester, all residents will be provided with a $25 print allotment on their USCard. This allowance can only be used at USC Housing locations. Residents can also use USCard Discretionary funds at the printer once their Housing print allotment has been used.
In order to receive and use the print allotment, you must be a current USC Housing resident. You will first need to log into housingprint.usc.edu with your USC Net ID credentials in order to activate the funds. The print $25 allotment is renewed each semester for current residents. Funds do not carry over and are non-refundable.

chunks.title: Housing Fees | USC Housing
chunks.text:
Application Processing Fee
A $65 nonrefundable application processing fee must be made at the time you submit your housing application. Please see the Application and Assignment menu for more information on how to apply. (Returning residents participating in our renewal process will have this fee charged to their student account.)
Contract Confirmation Payment
A $800 confirmation payment must be made at the time you confirm your contract. See Contracts. (Returning residents participating in our renewal process will have this fee charged to their student account.)
The confirmation payment for contracts for the spring and summer terms is $400.
The contract confirmation payment will be credited back to the student’s account if the resident fulfills the terms of their contract.
Rent
Housing charges are billed in two ways:
Rents for residence halls, suites and all undergraduate apartments, as well as meal plan costs, are billed at the beginning of each semester (August and December). You can set up a payment plan with the university Cashier’s office if you wish to pay your rent monthly.

chunks.title: Housing Fees | USC Housing
chunks.text:
nning of each semester (August and December). You can set up a payment plan with the university Cashier’s office if you wish to pay your rent monthly.
Rents for graduate student building and family housing are billed monthly. Charges appear on each monthly statement issued by the university Cashier’s Office.
Early Arrival
Students who have been approved to check into their housing assignments early will be charged a fee of $75 per night for each night prior to the beginning of their contract.
Live-Through
Residents staying in university housing between the end of a academic year contract and the beginning of a summer contract and/or the end of a summer housing contract and the beginning of an academic year contract will be charged a fee of $50 for each night.
Authorized Late Vacate
Residents approved to stay in university housing beyond the end of their contract will be charged a fee of $75 per night for each approved night stayed after the end of the contract.
Unauthorized Late Vacate

In addition to this fee, residents who remain beyond the end of their contract or approved extension may also be subject to other student conduct or legal action as well as other charges.

chunks.title: TV Connection | USC Housing
chunks.text:
Instructions
Most modern televisions require only the simplest of installation activity to work. Before you contact your service center, please read and follow these steps:
Make sure the television is connected to AC power, and to the cable outlet. The cable outlet requires a coaxial cable that will connect into the outlet and the TV. This is a round cable that can be any length.
If you have a remote control, make sure the batteries are good.
If you do not receive all of the channels listed on the channel lineup, your TV may need to be set up and programmed to be cable ready.
With slight variations, all modern televisions require similar actions to prepare for use with a cable system. If the exact term listed below is not on your programming menu, there probably is a very similar term.
Go to “MENU”, “Programming”, or “Action” screen.
From this screen, go to “Set-Up”.
If you are prompted to choose between “off-Air” and “Cable”, chose “Cable”.
Go to “Auto Program”.
When you depress the “Auto Program” button your television will begin to automatically scroll through the channels. The TV is programming itself to acquire the channels that have signal coming from the cable TV system.

chunks.title: TV Connection | USC Housing
chunks.text:
n to automatically scroll through the channels. The TV is programming itself to acquire the channels that have signal coming from the cable TV system.
Save the changes and exit.
Alternate: Some TV’s (typically older ones) have an “antenna-CATV” switch on the back. Be sure this is in the “CATV” position.
If you do not have reception after you have tried these steps. notify your Customer Service Center. They will direct you in additional steps or dispatch a service person as soon as possible. Please note, that it may take a day or two to attend to your request as there may be other requests ahead of you.

The production environment supports live applications and requires separate access. Production usage costs are charged to the sponsoring department or research project.

chunks.text:
Click to Download pdf version
ITS Mission
Information Technology Services is committed to delivering innovative, sustainable, and people-centric technology solutions.
Strategic Priorities
Advance Emerging Technologies – Expand access to artificial intelligence and modern solutions to support USC’s academic, research, and administrative needs.
Operational Excellence – Streamline processes and consolidate services to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and enhance service delivery.
Risk Reduction – Strengthen cybersecurity, compliance, and business continuity to protect the institution and minimize exposure.
Enterprise Goals
Artificial Intelligence Position ITS as USC’s central hub for secure, centralized AI services by enabling enterprise access to AI tools that foster a university-wide culture of operational efficiency and data-driven decision making.
Service & Portfolio Delivery Increase customer trust in ITS by delivering reliable, high-quality services, consistent measurement, and unified project management for greater visibility, accountability, and value.

delivering reliable, high-quality services, consistent measurement, and unified project management for greater visibility, accountability, and value.
Risk Management & Cybersecurity Mature our cybersecurity and risk posture by managing risks, maintaining compliance, business continuity, and a culture of shared responsibility.
Research Computing Strengthen USC’s computational and data ecosystem to enable leadership in AI-driven research and innovation by enhancing research IT capacity, ensuring sustainability, and fostering cross-divisional collaboration.
Continuous Improvement Drive continuous improvement through automation and root-cause elimination to reduce operational effort and reinvest capacity in higher-value initiatives.
Talent Management Accelerate ITS’ talent management maturity by engaging all ITS leaders in evaluating organizational skills, mitigating staffing and succession risks, and growing the capabilities and career development for all ITS staff.

Important Update for Federal Loan Borrowers Beginning July 1, 2026
Federal loan programs are changing under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Some figures below (interest rates, annual/aggregate loan limits, and repayment-plan details) reflect rules in effect before July 1, 2026, and do not apply to new borrowers or new loans disbursed on or after that date.
On This Page
Jump to a Section
Loans
Many students and families borrow from federal and private loan programs to assist in financing a college education. Loans are considered a valuable resource in helping students attain their educational goals. Management and repayment of loans become the student’s and/or family’s responsibility once the student graduates.
Regardless of lender, loans must be repaid with interest and, in many cases, include additional fees to obtain (origination fees). Do not take on more debt than you can handle. Borrow only what you need.
Funding Your College Education

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid
chunks.text:
additional fees to obtain (origination fees). Do not take on more debt than you can handle. Borrow only what you need.
Funding Your College Education
Pursuing a college degree, whether at the undergraduate or graduate level, represents a significant commitment of time and money. Besides tuition, you will need to ensure that you have enough to cover basic living expenses such as housing and food, in addition to personal expenses. If you borrow loans to cover these costs, your financial commitment will last well beyond graduation.
The USC Advantage
Students at USC enjoy all the resources of a large research university and the feel of a smaller liberal arts college. With small class sizes; world-class faculty who are leading experts in their fields; a broad range of research opportunities; and all the cultural, professional and entertainment possibilities that Los Angeles has to offer, you will graduate well-prepared for the realities of the 21st century.
How Your Financial Aid Data Is Used

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid

How Your Financial Aid Data Is Used
Once you have secured your student loans, information regarding them is tracked by the National Student Loan Data System, which serves as a central clearinghouse and is accessible via studentaid.gov. You can log in to the site using your FSA ID to review the loans you’ve borrowed, their account balances, repayment plans, and loan servicers. Your data is kept secure and is used only for the purposes of providing you information about your loans and maintaining the integrity of federal Title IV programs.

Loans for Undergraduate Students
USC participates in the Federal Direct Loan Program, which offers low-interest loans to undergraduate students and their parents. Loans are backed by the U.S. government. Your eligibility is determined by the financial information provided in your FAFSA and the cost of attendance at your college or university.
Loans for Undergraduate Students and Their Parents
Direct Subsidized Loans: Based on financial need, as determined by the information in your FAFSA.
Direct Unsubsidized Loans: Based on your cost of attendance, less other aid you receive.

Federal Direct Loans
Federal Direct Loans are available to most eligible borrowers who apply for financial aid.
Eligibility
You may be eligible for a Direct Loan if you:
Are enrolled at least half-time.
Are enrolled in the number of units indicated in your financial aid summary.
Maintain satisfactory academic progress (SAP) toward your degree objective.
Read more about the SAP policy for undergraduates or the SAP policy for graduate students.

How to Apply
To learn more, please view our “Applying for Direct Loans at USC” video.
Complete ALL six steps to receive your Direct Loan:
Step 1. Complete and submit the Free Application for Student Aid (FAFSA) as soon as possible, even if the priority date has already passed.
Step 2. Log in to your FAST portal and complete the Federal Direct Subsidized and/or Subsidized Direct Loan Request form found in the “Document Library.”
Undergraduate students must wait to receive their financial aid summary before they submit the form.
Graduate students may complete the form at any time.
The Financial Aid Office will email you confirmation once we process your loan and notify the Department of Education.
You can check your financial aid status at any time by logging in to your FAST portal.
Step 3. Sign your Master Promissory Note (MPN) online at studentaid.gov.
You will need the FSA ID issued to you by the Department of Education when you completed your FAFSA. If you have forgotten your FSA ID, you can retrieve it through studentaid.gov.

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid

You can check the status of your MPN by logging in to your FAST portal.
You will not be required to complete a new MPN if you previously borrowed a Direct Loan at another school and your existing MPN is no more than 10 years old.
Step 4. You must complete entrance loan counseling online at usc.igrad.com if you are:
A first-time undergraduate or graduate borrower at USC, or
A new graduate student who borrowed at USC as an undergraduate student.
Step 5. First-time undergraduate borrowers must complete additional loan counseling through iGrad.

New borrowing limits effective July 1, 2026
The information below does not reflect recent changes to federal loan availability and limits for new borrowers resulting from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. For parents who take out a Parent PLUS Loan on behalf of a dependent student on or after July 1, 2026, annual borrowing will be capped at $20,000 per student, with a lifetime limit of $65,000 per dependent student. Parents who borrowed before this date and whose student remains enrolled in the same program may continue under existing limits for up to three additional years. Parents who wish to access an income-based repayment plan should be aware that consolidation into a Direct Consolidation Loan must occur before July 1, 2026, with enrollment in a qualifying repayment plan completed before July 1, 2028. Parent PLUS borrowers who miss these deadlines, or who take out new loans on or after July 1, 2026, will not be eligible for income-based repayment. For more information, please visit our OBBBA page.

Eligibility
These loans are available only to parent borrowers wishing to fund all or part of their eligible student’s undergraduate studies. It is not based on the student’s financial need. No collateral is required, but a credit check is performed. Applicants’ credit history must be free of seriously adverse items, such as collection accounts, charge-offs and bankruptcy. Please review the credit requirements on the Federal Student Aid website.
Students must meet the following requirements:
Considered a dependent for the purposes of receiving federal need-based aid.
Enrolled at least half-time (6 units) in undergraduate status.
Enrolled in the number of units indicated in their financial aid summary.
Submit all documents required by the Financial Aid Office.
Maintain satisfactory academic progress.
Parents and students must meet the following requirements:
Parents and students must be U.S. citizens or eligible non-citizens.
The parent must be the biological or adoptive parent, or stepparent, of the student.

The Graduate PLUS Loan program is ending for new borrowers beginning July 1, 2026. Graduate students who had a federal loan disbursement before that date and remain continuously enrolled in the same program may continue borrowing Graduate PLUS funds for up to three additional years, or until program completion, whichever comes first. Parent PLUS Loan — new borrowing limits effective July 1, 2026
For parents who take out a Parent PLUS Loan on behalf of a dependent student on or after July 1, 2026, annual borrowing will be capped at $20,000 per student, with a lifetime limit of $65,000 per dependent student. Parents who borrowed before this date and whose student remains enrolled in the same program may continue under existing limits for up to three additional years. Parents who wish to access an income-based repayment plan should be aware that consolidation into a Direct Consolidation Loan must occur before July 1, 2026, with enrollment in a qualifying repayment plan completed before July 1, 2028. Parent PLUS borrowers who miss these deadlines, or who take out new loans on or after July 1, 2026, will not be eligible for income-based repayment.

Federal Loan Repayment Protections
One of the most significant advantages of federal borrowing is access to repayment protections that private loans do not offer. Beginning July 1, 2026, a new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) will replace most existing income-driven plans for loans disbursed on or after that date. Under RAP, monthly payments are based on income and family size, ranging from 1% to 10% of adjusted gross income, with loan forgiveness available after 30 years of qualifying payments. Borrowers with loans taken out before July 1, 2026 may remain on current plans — including Income-Based Repayment, Graduated, and Extended repayment — or elect to move into RAP. Eligible borrowers may also qualify for Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), which forgives remaining federal loan balances after 10 years of qualifying payments in public service employment. None of these options are available on private loans.

Limitations of Private Loans
Private student loans cannot be included in a Federal Direct Consolidation Loan and are not eligible for federal income-driven repayment plans, Public Service Loan Forgiveness, or federal economic hardship deferment protections. They generally carry higher interest rates and offer fewer borrower protections than federal loans.

Your student loan is real money. You have to pay it back, so borrow wisely.
When you accept a loan, you accept legal and financial responsibilities that last until the loan is repaid. Loans must be repaid with interest, which begins to accrue when you:
Receive your initial loan disbursement; or
Cease to be enrolled in school at least half-time.

Establish good credit by repaying your student loan. Paying your student loan on time affords you the chance to build a solid credit history that will help define the course of your life. On the other hand, defaulting on your loan can have serious, long-term consequences.
When you accept a student loan, you agree to:
Repay your loan, including accrued interest and fees, whether or not you complete your education, complete the program within the regular time frame, obtain employment or are satisfied with your education.

Student Loan Advisory
All borrowers should be aware of the following:
Borrowing a loan is a way to use your future income to meet today’s needs. Every dollar borrowed will be repaid with interest out of your future income.
Borrow only what you need. Students are not required to borrow the full amount offered in their financial aid summary.
Before spending, ask yourself:

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid

Borrow only what you need. Students are not required to borrow the full amount offered in their financial aid summary.
Before spending, ask yourself:
Does this meet a basic need?
Is this greatly enhancing my quality of life?
Is this an investment in my future?
Investigate other sources of financial aid that do not need to be repaid, such as scholarships and Federal Work-Study.
To reduce total debt, students can try to make some interest payments on Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans and Federal Direct PLUS Loans while they are at USC or covered by a grace period. Or, just borrow less.
Inform the loan servicer when changing your name or address, or if you withdraw or graduate from USC.
Establish good credit by wisely managing loan repayments. Make all payments on time (consider setting up automatic payments from your checking account) and keep copies of all documents and correspondence.
Reduce the cost of the investment in education by focusing on needs instead of wants. Wherever possible, students should eliminate those expenditures that do not meet life’s necessities.

Ombudsman
An ombudsman is an independent, neutral official authorized to investigate and resolve disputes between individuals and public agencies or authorities. The Federal Student Aid (FSA) Ombudsman acts on the behalf of loan borrowers to conduct informal, impartial investigations into complaints against loan agencies, servicers and companies. They will recommend solutions, but they do not have the authority to reverse decisions. They will also work to institute changes that will prevent future problems for other student loan borrowers. This free service is provided by the U.S. Department of Education.
The Ombudsman will research your complaint and determine if you have been treated fairly. If your student loan complaint is justified, they will work with you and the office, agency, or company involved. They will also contact other offices within the U.S. Department of Education, your private lender, your loan guaranty agency, and the servicing agency or firm collecting your loan.

Compliance
The following memorializes the USC Office of Financial Aid Code of Conduct and Business Practices for Relationships with Lenders (Code of Conduct) that should apply in our relationships with any lending institution that is an actual or potential lender to USC students and parents. This Code of Conduct applies to all managers and employees in the University Park Financial Aid Office and all financial aid managers and employees in the professional schools (Financial Aid Employees).

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid
chunks.text:
loyees in the University Park Financial Aid Office and all financial aid managers and employees in the professional schools (Financial Aid Employees).
1. No Payments to Financial Aid Officers and Employees: Financial Aid Employees may not accept anything of more than nominal value (less than $50.00 per year or an isolated lunch or dinner) from any lending institution. This standard also applies to gifts, meals and other business courtesies.
2. No Significant Equity Interests: Financial Aid Employees may not hold a significant public or private equity interest (e.g., stocks, stock options, warrants or other ownership interests) in any lending institution that is on the university’s lender list. A “significant” interest does not include any mutual funds or other equity interests that are managed by a third party or investments representing less than 1 percent of the total equity of a publicly traded entity.

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid
chunks.text:
er equity interests that are managed by a third party or investments representing less than 1 percent of the total equity of a publicly traded entity.
3. Service on an Advisory Board Requires Approval: Financial Aid Employees may not serve on an advisory board, commission, or group established by any lending institution or group of institutions without obtaining prior written approval from the Provost or his/her designee. Financial Aid Employees may not receive any reimbursement or other compensation for serving on an approved advisory board, commission, or group. Lending institutions shall not pay for any travel, food or lodging expenses incurred as a result of service on an advisory board.
4. No Compensation for Consulting: Financial Aid Employees may not accept any fee, payment, or other financial benefit from any lending institution as compensation for any type of consulting arrangement or contract to provide services to or on behalf of the lender relating to education loans.

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid
chunks.text:
tion as compensation for any type of consulting arrangement or contract to provide services to or on behalf of the lender relating to education loans.
5. No Remuneration to the University: Financial Aid Employees may not accept or receive anything of value from a lending institution on behalf of or as a representative of USC, in exchange for any advantage or consideration given to the lending institution. This prohibition includes, but is not limited to, revenue-sharing arrangements, scholarships, reimbursement for printing costs or services, equipment offered at less than fair market value and staffing assistance. “Revenue-sharing arrangement” means an arrangement between USC and a lender under which the lender provides private education loans to students attending USC (or the families of those students), USC recommends the lender or their loan products and, in exchange, the lender pays a fee or provides other material benefit, including revenue or profit sharing, to USC or to its officers, employees, or agents.

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid
chunks.text:
hange, the lender pays a fee or provides other material benefit, including revenue or profit sharing, to USC or to its officers, employees, or agents.
6. No Offer of Funds for Private Loans: Financial Aid Employees shall not request or accept from any lender any offer of funds to be used for private education loans (as defined in section 140 of the Truth in Lending Act), including funds for an opportunity pool loan, to students in exchange for the university providing concessions or promises to the lender for a specific number of loans made, insured or guaranteed; a specified loan volume; or a preferred lender arrangement. An “opportunity pool loan” is defined as a private education loan made by a lender to a student (or the student’s family) that involves a payment by the institution of points, premiums, additional interest, or financial support to the lender for the purpose of extending credit to the student or the family.
7. Lender Lists Must Serve Students and Parents: Lender lists must be based solely on the best interests of the students or parents, who may use the list without regard to the financial interests of the university.

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid
chunks.text:
st be based solely on the best interests of the students or parents, who may use the list without regard to the financial interests of the university.
8. Lender List Disclosure: USC will clearly disclose the process and criteria used to select those lending institutions that appear on its lender lists and related brochures or websites. Students must be told that they have the right and ability to select the lending institution of their choice, regardless of the lender lists. The lender lists and their selection criteria shall be reviewed and published at least annually.
9. Directing Borrowers to Lenders: Financial Aid Employees may not direct borrowers to particular lenders or refuse or delay loan certifications based on the borrower’s choice of lender. For any first-time borrower, USC may not assign, through the award packaging or other methods, the borrower’s loan to a particular lender.
10. Prohibition on Staffing Assistance: Financial Aid Employees may not request or accept any assistance from any lending institution with call center staffing to respond to financial aid inquiries by USC parents or staff or financial aid office staffing.

chunks.title: Loans - Financial Aid

from any lending institution with call center staffing to respond to financial aid inquiries by USC parents or staff or financial aid office staffing.
11. Transparency in Employment: Employees of lending institutions must clearly identify that they are employed by a lending institution when interacting with USC students and parents. Employees of lending institutions are not permitted to identify themselves as USC employees to USC students and parents.
12. Entrance/Exit Counseling: Financial Aid Employees will not engage any lending institution to provide entrance or exit counseling to USC students.
The Provost or his/her designee will review this Code of Conduct and may update or revise it at his/her discretion to ensure that it remains current and consistent with university policy and regulatory requirements.

To qualify for work-study, you must demonstrate financial need, meet all application deadlines, be a U.S. citizen or eligible noncitizen and enroll for the number of units your financial aid award was based on.
You will need to find a job in order to receive the funds.
Finding a Job
Most approved Federal Work-Study jobs are available on campus. We encourage you to apply to the ones that interest you and/or that complement your academic or career goals.
Campus job openings are advertised on Handshake, a service of the Career Center, and in the Daily Trojan. Jobs can also be found on flyers posted around campus and through word of mouth. Many USC departments accept walk-in applicants.
Held the Friday before the first week of each semester, the annual USC Job Fair is an excellent opportunity to look for an on-campus job. To register, please visit the Handshake website.
You will need to present your Social Security card and driver’s license or passport. Be sure to bring these with you from home to avoid any delays in the hiring process.
